questions.question: 1. What is the standard etchant used for observing the microstructure of plain carbon steel?

explanations.a: Incorrect — ferric chloride is mainly used for etching non-ferrous metals like copper and its alloys, not standard for plain carbon steel.
explanations.b: Correct — Nital (a solution of nitric acid in alcohol) is the standard etchant for plain carbon steel, commonly used to reveal ferrite-pearlite structures.
explanations.c: Incorrect — hydrofluoric acid is highly dangerous and typically used for silicon-containing materials, not standard steel microstructure etching.
explanations.d: Incorrect — sulfuric acid is not used as a standard metallographic etchant for steel microstructure observation.

questions.question: 2. What two phases would you expect to see in the microstructure of a slowly cooled hypoeutectoid steel?

explanations.a: Incorrect — ferrite and cementite together as separate bulk phases are not the typical equilibrium microstructure; cementite mainly exists within pearlite.
explanations.b: Incorrect — austenite is not present at room temperature after slow cooling; it transforms into ferrite and pearlite.
explanations.c: Correct — slowly cooled hypoeutectoid steel consists of proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite.
explanations.d: Incorrect — cementite is not a primary phase in hypoeutectoid steel; pearlite already contains cementite in lamellar form.

questions.question: 3. Which of the following image is a structure of ‘annealed’ condition of a 0.45 %C hypoeutectoid steel?

explanations.a: Incorrect — does not match the typical annealed hypoeutectoid structure of ferrite + pearlite balance.
explanations.b: Correct — shows the annealed 0.45% C hypoeutectoid steel microstructure consisting of proeutectoid ferrite (light regions) and pearlite colonies (dark lamellar regions), which is characteristic of slow cooling/annealing.
explanations.c: Incorrect — likely represents a different heat-treated or non-equilibrium structure, not annealed condition.
explanations.d: Incorrect — does not represent the expected ferrite–pearlite equilibrium microstructure of annealed steel.

questions.question: 4. The distinguishing microstructural feature of nodular cast iron (or ductile iron) is the presence of:

explanations.a: Incorrect — graphite flakes are characteristic of gray cast iron, not ductile (nodular) iron.
explanations.b: Incorrect — cementite needles are not the defining feature of nodular cast iron microstructure.
explanations.c: Correct — ductile (nodular) cast iron is characterized by graphite spheroids (nodules), which improve strength and ductility.
explanations.d: Incorrect — temper carbon nodules are associated with malleable cast iron, not nodular (ductile) cast iron.

questions.question: 5. The matrix microstructure of as-cast nodular iron can consist of:

answers.d: Ferrite, pearlite, or a mixture of both with graphite

explanations.a: Incorrect — as-cast nodular iron does not consist of pure cementite; cementite is not the main matrix phase.
explanations.b: Incorrect — the matrix is not always only ferrite; it depends on cooling rate and composition.
explanations.c: Incorrect — it is not exclusively pearlite; ferrite may also be present in the matrix.
explanations.d: Correct — the matrix of as-cast nodular iron can be ferritic, pearlitic, or a ferrite–pearlite mixture, with graphite nodules dispersed in it.

questions.question: 6. For brass with approximately 40% zinc (Muntz metal), what is the typical microstructure at room temperature?

answers.c: A mixture of alpha (α) and beta (𝛽′) phases

explanations.a: Incorrect — pure alpha phase occurs at lower zinc contents (up to ~35% Zn), not at ~40% Zn.
explanations.b: Incorrect — beta (β′) phase alone is not stable at room temperature in this composition; it usually appears with alpha in two-phase region.
explanations.c: Correct — at ~40% Zn (Muntz metal), the microstructure at room temperature is a mixture of alpha (α) and beta (β′) phases.
explanations.d: Incorrect — it is not a single homogeneous solid solution because the composition lies in the two-phase α + β region.
